title: Steamed Sweet Potatoes with Groundnut Sauce
author: Nabwile Joyce
desc: Sweet potatoes wrapped in banana leaves and steamed over half an hour on a bed of banana stems, with a groundnut sauce built from tomato and onion boiled in water and thickened with paste mixed cold.
longDesc: This is the signature Busoga pairing, and it is the clearest written example of the leaf-steaming that the kingdom is known for — steaming food is a popular way of cooking in Busoga, and the rig is banana stems in water with a leaf laid over them. The potatoes go on top in their own leaf parcel, covered with another leaf. The sauce follows the universal Ugandan rule: tomato and onion boiled first, groundnut paste mixed with cold water to a fluid consistency and only then stirred in.
equipment: Deep pan with a tight lid
Mortar and pestle, for pounding the peanuts
steps: Peel, cut and wash the sweet potatoes.
Place banana stems in a pan with water.
Layer a banana leaf over the water-covered stems.
Wrap the sweet potatoes in banana leaves and set them on the leaf, then cover the pan with another leaf.
Pound the peanuts into a paste, or use ready-made paste.
Boil the tomatoes and onions with water.
Mix the peanut paste with cold water to a fluid consistency.
Add it to the boiling liquid and simmer, stirring, until thick.
Serve the potatoes with the sauce.
chefTips: Banana stems in the water, a leaf over them, the parcel on top, another leaf as the lid. That layered rig is the Busoga steaming method and it is worth learning as a technique rather than as one recipe.
Over thirty minutes is the source's own phrasing, and it means what it says — this is not a twenty-minute job.
Mix the groundnut paste with cold water to a fluid consistency before it goes in. Every Ugandan groundnut sauce turns on this and the ones that go lumpy skipped it.
Boil the tomatoes and onions in water first. The paste goes into a hot liquid, not the other way round.
Pounding the peanuts yourself is said to release the oils better than machine grinding, and it is the traditional preference.
Simmer and stir until thick. That is the only doneness cue given and it is enough.
No quantities are documented. One figure in the source — about 100 kg of sweet potato — is annual consumption per person, not a recipe quantity, and it should not be mistaken for one.

Busoga is a Bantu kingdom and one of four constitutional monarchies in Uganda, ruled by an elected Kyabazinga. Its food is thinly documented and mostly served by tour-operator pages, which is why this chapter matters.
commonMistakes: Letting the water touch the potato parcel.
Mixing the groundnut paste into hot liquid.
Reading the 100 kg consumption figure as an ingredient quantity.
sources: Adapted from the Busoga chapter of the Wikibooks project 'Mujje Tulye from Uganda' — the banana-stems-in-water rig with a leaf layered over them, the wrapped potato parcel, the covering leaf, the over-30-minute steam, and the groundnut sauce method of pounding the peanuts, boiling tomatoes and onions with water, mixing the paste with cold water to a fluid consistency and simmering while stirring until thick are all from that chapter. It states explicitly that it gives no quantities.

That chapter also records that Busoga is a traditional Bantu kingdom and one of four constitutional monarchies in present-day Uganda, ruled by an elected Kyabazinga, and that steaming food is a popular way of cooking in Busoga.
Its figure of about 100 kg of sweet potato is annual per-capita consumption, not a recipe quantity, and is flagged as such rather than used.
The Wikibooks category page omits this chapter entirely and under-reports its own contents, so it was recovered by search rather than from the index.
The preference for mortar-and-pestle pounding over machine grinding to better release the oils is from 'Ebinyebwa; a tale of the Ugandan groundnut stew', Daily Monitor, 7 April 2012.
storage: Refrigerate up to 3 days. Keep the sauce and potatoes separate.
reheating: Steam the potatoes; warm the sauce with a splash of water.
healthBenefits: Sweet potatoes are high in fibre, potassium and vitamin C.
Groundnut paste supplies plant protein, niacin, folate and vitamin E.
Steaming preserves more of the potatoes' nutrients than boiling.
culturalNote: Busoga is fishing and farming country around Jinja, and it is one of the worst-documented food regions in Uganda despite being one of its four kingdoms — most of what is online about it comes from safari operators. That its one properly written chapter is about steaming sweet potatoes says something about what has and has not been recorded.
